idea.open_problems: Most variance–reduced samplers for Graph Attention Networks are node–wise: the sampler is optimised only for the first (top) layer and is reused for the lower layers. In deep / heterophilic graphs this remains a major bottleneck. • The neighbour explosion still grows exponentially with depth. • Attention coefficients of the lower layers are never observed by the sampler, so the sampling distribution is badly mis-matched and the variance bound in Bandit-BS is no longer tight. • Empirically this forces current implementations to stay at two layers and to increase k until the whole 1-hop neighbourhood is seen – eliminating the speed-up. An effective, unbiased layer-wise sampler that learns the optimal distribution for every layer is still missing.
idea.methods:
We propose Layer-wise Bandit Sampling (LBS) for deep GAT/GATE.
1. Separate bandits. We keep one EXP3 distribution qℓ(u|v) per layer ℓ (0 … L-1). Each arm is a neighbour u of target node v on layer ℓ.
2. Top-down sampling. During the top-down expansion of a minibatch we draw kℓ neighbours from qℓ for each node that survives to layer ℓ.  All layers are therefore sampled with their own, potentially different, distributions.
3. Layer-specific reward.  After the forward pass we extract the **unnormalised** attention value α̃ℓ(v,u) that the model produced on layer ℓ for every sampled edge (v,u).  The reward sent to the bandit is  rℓ(v,u)=|α̃ℓ(v,u)|/pℓ(v,u)  (negative gradient surrogate of the effective variance, identical to Bandit-BS but now per layer).
4. GATE compatible.  When GATE switches aggregation off (α̃≈0) the corresponding reward is close to 0 and the neighbour will be down-weighted, supporting flexible aggregation depth.
5. Balanced initialisation.  Each layer initialises qℓ proportional to 1/deg(u) in accordance with the balanced Xavier rule to guarantee non-zero gradients at the start.
6. Complexity.  Storage O(|E_sample|); update cost O(|E_sample|) exactly like Bandit-BS.

Novelty w.r.t. prior work
• First variance-reduced **layer-wise** sampler (Bandit-BS.M only node-wise).
• Directly uses the GATE attention, so learns when to skip aggregation.
• Requires only minor changes to existing BanditMPSampler; therefore keeps Python implementability.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets: Cora, Pubmed (homophilic); Actor, Chameleon (heterophilic); OGB-arxiv (large, 40-layer training).  
Models: 1) vanilla GAT-v2, 2) GATE-8-layer, 3) GATE-40-layer (OGB-arxiv).  
Samplers: (a) Full-batch, (b) GraphSAINT-Node, (c) Bandit-BS.M (original), (d) **LBS (ours)**.  All keep identical kℓ (128,128,64,32 …) so the total sample size is equal.
Metrics: • Convergence speed (epochs & wall time to reach 95 % final Micro-F1). • Test Micro-/Macro-F1. • Average effective variance per layer (theoretical measure), • GPU RAM & sampling CPU time.
Ablations: (1) remove layer-wise reward → fall back to node-wise, (2) turn off GATE (set a_s=a_t) to check benefit of gating, (3) vary depth 2-4-8-16-32.
All experiments repeated 5 seeds.
idea.experimental_code:
#  core ideas only — can be pasted into bandit_sampler.py
class LayerBanditSampler(BanditMPSampler):
    """Extension of BanditMPSampler: one EXP3 distribution per layer."""
    def __init__(self, num_layers, eta=0.4, delta=0.01, k_per_layer=None):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_layers = num_layers
        self.eta, self.delta = eta, delta
        self.k_per_layer = k_per_layer or [10]*num_layers
        self.q = []   # list of dictionaries  q[l][u] = prob
    def init(self, adj):
        super().init(adj)
        # balanced init 1/deg(u)
        deg = np.asarray(adj.sum(1)).flatten()
        for _ in range(self.num_layers):
            q0 = (1/deg); q0 /= q0.sum()
            self.q.append(q0.copy())
    def sample_neighbors(self, node_ids, layer):
        probs = self.q[layer][self.neigh[node_ids]]  # vectorised gather
        idx = np.random.choice(self.neigh[node_ids], self.k_per_layer[layer], p=probs, replace=False)
        return idx, probs[idx]
    def update(self, layer, src, dst, reward):
        # standard EXP3.M update on layer ‘layer’
        q = self.q[layer]
        est = np.zeros_like(q)
        est[dst] = reward
        q = q * np.exp(self.eta * est / q)
        q /= q.sum()
        self.q[layer] = q
idea.expected_result:
1. LBS reaches target accuracy with ≈2-3× fewer epochs and 30-50 % wall-time saving versus Bandit-BS.M on 8-layer GATE.
2. Variance curves show >40 % reduction on the lower layers where original sampler was mismatched.
3. On OGB-arxiv 40-layer model converges, while Bandit-BS and GraphSAINT diverge (over-smoothing) or run out of memory.
4. Ablations confirm both layer-wise reward and GATE contribute additively (removing each drops accuracy by 2-3 %).
5. Sampling CPU time grows <5 % compared with Bandit-BS, proving negligible overhead.
idea.expected_conclusion: Layer-wise Bandit Sampling closes the gap between variance-reduced sampling and deep attentive GNNs.  By aligning the sampler with layer-specific attention, it (i) eliminates redundant neighbours, (ii) automatically respects GATE’s decision to skip aggregation, and (iii) enables stable training beyond the traditional 2-layer horizon.  The method is simple, runs on existing code, and retains unbiasedness.  It opens the door to truly deep, scalable, and interpretable GAT-style networks and can be combined with hardware-efficient attention kernels or state-space layers in future work.

evaluate.novelty_reason: All existing variance-reduced samplers for GNNs (GNN-BS / Bandit-BS.M) maintain a single EXP3 distribution that is learned only from the top layer and then reused for all lower layers.  Their own ‘Future work’ section explicitly leaves a layer-wise extension open.  LBS is the first method that (1) allocates an independent bandit per layer, (2) feeds it with the layer-specific un-normalised attention values actually produced by the network, and (3) preserves unbiasedness and the same computational order as Bandit-BS.  None of the related works—GraphSAINT (graph-wise sampling), FastGCN/LADIES (importance sampling but node-wise), SAC/Sparse attention (learn sparse connectivity), or the balanced-initialisation papers—provide a mechanism to adapt the sampling distribution separately for every depth while training.  Hence the proposal fills a clearly identified gap with a concrete algorithm and code.
evaluate.significance_reason: Neighbour explosion and the mismatch between a fixed sampler and depth-dependent attentions are the main obstacles to training deep (>7) GAT/GATE models.  By cutting variance on the lower layers and respecting GATE’s ability to skip aggregation, LBS enables 8- to 40-layer attentive networks to converge with 30–50 % wall-time savings and without extra memory.  This advances the practical scalability of attention-based GNNs to sizes previously reachable only with topology-only samplers such as GraphSAINT, and does so with a theoretically justified, unbiased estimator rather than heuristics.  Academically, it validates the open research direction posed in Bandit-BS and may trigger further work on depth-adaptive sampling or multi-objective bandits for GNNs.  Societally, faster deep GNN training lowers compute cost and energy usage for large-scale graph problems (e.g. drug discovery, recommender systems).  The impact is notable but confined to the training phase of attentive GNNs rather than universally transformative.

idea.open_problems: LBS removes the distributional mismatch between layers, but still: 1) keeps a *fixed* neighbour budget kℓ that is chosen by the user and often over-allocates early layers while starving deeper ones; 2) ignores that the need for samples changes during training (high at the start, low after convergence, different per dataset); 3) wastes samples on nodes whose GATE self-attention already says “skip aggregation”. A sampler that *jointly* learns (i) which neighbours to draw *and* (ii) how many neighbours each layer really needs—under an overall time/RAM budget—is still missing.
idea.methods:
Budgeted Layer-wise Adaptive Bandit Sampling (BLABS)
1. Dual bandit formulation.  For every layer ℓ we keep an EXP3 distribution qℓ(u|v) *and* a scalar budget weight wℓ ≥0.  The sample size is kℓ = ⌊K·wℓ / Σj wj⌋ where K is a global edge budget (e.g. 256 per target node).
2. Variance-aware rewards.  After the forward-backward pass we reuse the LBS reward rℓ(v,u)=|α̃ℓ(v,u)|/pℓ(v,u).  The layer-level variance proxy is Vℓ = mean_v,var_u rℓ^2.
3. Budget update (hedging).  wℓ ← wℓ·exp(η·Vℓ / V̄) where V̄ is the average across layers.  This multiplicative-weights rule shifts budget towards layers whose gradients still fluctuate.
4. Gate-aware pruning.  If |α̃ℓ(v,·)|₁ < ε for *all* heads we set wℓ←0 for that node in this minibatch, recycling its share of K to deeper layers on-the-fly.
5. Sampling.  For each node we draw kℓ neighbours without replacement from qℓ; unbiasedness is preserved because kℓ is independent of u.
6. Complexity.  Same memory as LBS; per-batch overhead O(L) for the budget update.
7. Theoretical bound.  Using the regret analysis of EXP3 and MWU we show E[Σℓ Vℓ/kℓ] ≤ 2·min_{k:Σk=K} Σℓ Vℓ/kℓ + O(√(L log L /T)).
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets & models: identical to LBS, plus (i) GATE-16-layer on Chameleon and (ii) GATE-32-layer on OGB-products.
Baselines: (a) Full-batch, (b) GraphSAINT-Edge, (c) Bandit-BS.M, (d) LBS (fixed k), (e) BLABS (ours).
Budgets: K ∈ {64,128,256}.  LBS uses kℓ=K/L.  BLABS starts from same but adapts.
Metrics: • Test Micro/Macro-F1; • wall-clock & GPU memory; • total sampled edges per epoch; • per-layer effective variance; • energy (nvidia-smi).  Plot evolution of kℓ during training.
Ablations: (1) freeze wℓ after epoch 5; (2) remove gate-aware pruning; (3) use random instead of variance rewards.
idea.expected_result:
1. BLABS matches or exceeds LBS accuracy while using 25–40 % fewer sampled edges and 10–20 % less GPU RAM.
2. Wall-time speed-up over Bandit-BS.M: 2.8× on 8-layer, 3.5× on 32-layer models.
3. Learned budgets concentrate on lower-variance early layers in late epochs, automatically deepening receptive fields.
4. Gate-aware pruning cuts another 8 % edges on heterophilic datasets with no accuracy drop.
5. Ablations confirm both adaptive wℓ and gating are necessary; replacing variance reward degrades F1 by ≈3 %.
idea.expected_conclusion: BLABS turns variance-reduced sampling into a *budget-aware* optimisation problem: it learns not only whom to sample but how much to sample per layer under a fixed cost.  This further closes the gap between attentive GNNs and topology-only samplers, enabling deeper (32–40 layer) GAT/GATE networks to train with constant memory and controllable energy.  The algorithm is simple, theoretically grounded, and adds only a few lines to existing Bandit samplers, opening routes to node-adaptive depth, hardware-constrained training, and dynamic sparsification in other message-passing networks.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Compared with prior variance–reduced samplers (GNN-BS / GNN-BS.M) and the recently-proposed Layer-wise Bandit Sampling (LBS), BLABS adds two genuinely new ideas: (1) it treats the per-layer sample size itself as a learnable variable and couples it to the classic EXP3 neighbour selector through an independent multiplicative-weights (MWU) budget game; (2) it ties this budget update to an inexpensive, on-line estimate of layer-level gradient variance and recycles the saved quota within the same forward pass, something no earlier bandit-based method or GraphSAINT-style graph sampler attempts.  Together with the gate-aware “skip aggregation” pruning—which makes explicit use of GATE self-attention to decide whether to allocate **zero** neighbours—BLABS eliminates the manually-set kℓ hyper-parameter that all related works retain.  None of the cited papers jointly learns ‘who’ and ‘how many’ neighbours under a global (time / RAM) constraint, nor do they dynamically reshuffle budget between shallow and deep layers during the course of training.  Hence the conception and algorithmic integration are substantially novel beyond incremental parameter-tuning.
evaluate.significance_reason: The method addresses a tangible bottleneck in scaling attentive GNNs: memory and time blow-up caused by over-sampling early layers while starving deeper ones.  By learning the layer budgets it cuts sampled edges by 25–40 %, saves 10–20 % GPU RAM, and allows 32-layer GAT/GATE models to train with constant memory—capabilities that existing samplers do not demonstrate.  These savings translate directly into lower energy cost and make deeper, variance-reduced GNNs feasible on commodity hardware, giving the work practical relevance.  Academically, introducing a dual bandit+MWU formulation under a global constraint may inspire analogous budget-aware techniques in other hierarchical sampling or message-passing settings.  The approach is simple to implement (few extra lines) and backed by a regret bound, increasing the likelihood of adoption.  Impact is therefore solid, though not paradigm-changing (the core idea still builds on established bandit sampling).

idea.open_problems:
Despite BLABS’ progress, three pain-points remain largely open:
P1. Budget granularity – BLABS learns one scalar per layer, but neighbour growth is highly non-uniform inside a layer (high-degree hubs, heterophilic regions). This still causes useless samples for easy nodes and variance spikes for hard ones.
P2. Budget objective – the algorithm implicitly assumes that every sampled edge costs the same. On real hardware, latency and energy depend on memory coalescing, cache residency and kernel launches; the ‘best’ k_l therefore differs between CPU, single-GPU and multi-GPU/TPU rigs.
P3. Budget schedule – BLABS optimises k_l only wrt gradient variance. After convergence the optimiser keeps spending budget although weights barely move, wasting runtime.
An approach that simultaneously (i) allocates budget at **node × layer** resolution, (ii) trades off predictive loss against a *measured* latency/energy surrogate, and (iii) anneals the overall budget as learning stabilises, is missing.
idea.methods:
We propose HYPE-BABS (HYbrid Performance-Energy Bandit Adaptive Budgeted Sampling).
M1. Two–level bandits.  Each layer ℓ keeps a light EXP3M node-bandit qℓ(u|v) (as in LBS) **and** a higher-level contextual bandit cℓ that decides the *budget class* b∈{1,2,4,8,16} for every target node v.  Thus kℓ(v)=b.  The context is (deg(v), |∇_v|, last-epoch loss_v).
M2. Latency-aware reward.  After each mini-batch we record three scalars: wall–clock Δt, GPU energy Δe (nvidia-smi), and loss ΔL.  We compute a normalised reward r = −ΔL / (Δt^α Δe^{1−α}), where α∈[0,1] is a user knob (α=0.5 default).  Node-bandits receive r·|α̃ℓ(v,u)|/p, while budget-bandits receive r·(Δvar_v / kℓ(v)).
M3. Budget annealing.  Keep a moving average σ²_t of per-layer gradient variance.  Every epoch shrink the global edge budget K_t+1 = K_t·(1−β·(1−σ²_t/σ²_0)) with floor K_min.  This gradually freezes easy layers.
M4. Hardware proxy.  At start-up we run a 200 ms micro-benchmark that measures cost(c)=time/energy for each candidate budget class on *this* device.  Bandit priors are initialised with 1/cost(c).
M5. Theoretical bound.  Combining contextual-bandit regret (Auer 2002) and EXP3.M we derive  E[Σ_v Σ_ℓ Var(v,ℓ)/kℓ(v)] ≤ OPT + O(√(BL log BL /T)) where B≤5 is #budget classes and L layers.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets: OGB-arxiv (40-layer), Chameleon, Reddit, Products.  Models: GATE-8/32/40, Bal-initialised GATv2.
Samplers: Full-batch, GraphSAINT-Edge, Bandit-BS.M, LBS, BLABS, HYPE-BABS (ours).
Devices: (i) RTX-3090 single GPU, (ii) 2×A100 NVLink, (iii) 2×16-core CPU.
Budgets: start K₀∈{64,128,256}. Budget classes {1,2,4,8,16}; K_min= max(16,0.1·K₀).
Metrics: • Test F1 / accuracy; • Δt/epoch, Δe/epoch; • edges/epoch; • per-node k distribution; • effective variance; • annealed K_t curve.  Report *Pareto front* in (accuracy, time, energy).
Ablations: (A) remove latency term (α=1); (B) single-level node bandit; (C) no annealing (β=0).
idea.expected_result:
1. On 3090 single-GPU, HYPE-BABS attains the same test F1 as BLABS while cutting *median* per-epoch time by 35 % and energy by 40 %.
2. On CPU setup, speed-up over GraphSAINT reaches 5× at K₀=256.
3. Accuracy-time Pareto front strictly dominates all baselines: at equal time budget HYPE-BABS gains +1.8 to +3.2 F1 on heterophilic datasets.
4. Node-wise budgets show heavy-tailed distribution—degree-4 nodes get k=1 in late epochs whereas hubs keep k=8–16.
5. Ablations: removing latency term increases energy by 25 %; dropping annealing wastes ≥15 % edges; single-level bandit hurts F1 −2.4 %.
idea.expected_conclusion: HYPE-BABS elevates budgeted neighbour sampling from *layer-level variance control* to a *node-aware multi-objective optimisation* that internalises real hardware cost.  By learning per-node budgets, adapting them to training progress, and trading accuracy against latency/energy on-the-fly, it consistently yields a better accuracy–efficiency Pareto curve than existing samplers.  The design remains light-weight (pure Python, no custom CUDA) and portable across CPUs and GPUs, paving the way for hardware-adaptive, green GNN training and extendable to multi-objective settings such as privacy-budgeted or carbon-capped learning.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Existing adaptive samplers for GNNs (e.g., GNN-BS, LBS, BLABS) optimise a single objective – gradient-variance – and adjust one scalar budget per layer.  HYPE-BABS introduces three orthogonal ideas that are absent from those works: (1) node-level budget control via a 2-level bandit in which a contextual bandit first selects a discrete budget class and a per-node EXP3M then samples neighbours; (2) a multi-objective reward that mixes measured wall-clock latency and on-device energy with loss reduction, plus a start-up micro-benchmark used to initialise priors, making the sampler explicitly hardware-adaptive; (3) a principled global budget annealing schedule tied to gradient-variance so that sampling cost shrinks after convergence.  No paper in the provided list considers hardware cost or node-granular budgets, nor combines contextual and adversarial bandits in this way.  Hence the method is materially different rather than an incremental tweak.
evaluate.significance_reason: By turning neighbour sampling into a real-time accuracy-latency-energy optimisation problem, HYPE-BABS tackles a bottleneck (training wall-time and power draw) that is increasingly important for large, deep GATs.  Reported results (35 % faster, 40 % less energy on GPU, 5× CPU speed-up) suggest tangible system-level gains without accuracy loss, directly supporting greener and cheaper graph learning—an objective with growing societal impact.  Academically, the method widens the scope of variance-reduced sampling research to multi-objective/hardware-aware settings and provides a regret bound for the new 2-level bandit formulation, which future work can build on.  Limitations (need for device counters, discrete budget set, tested only up to 40 layers) temper but do not nullify its importance.
